title: The Self That is Only the Self
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: In a Soto Zen dharma talk, IkuShun Desiree Webster emphasizes the importance of direct experience and mindfulness practice to reveal our true nature. By letting go of conceptualization and embracing upright posture in zazen, we can tap into a deeper sense of self that is connected with everything, beyond individual preferences and opinions. This understanding is not about achieving enlightenment, but rather about embracing the present moment and allowing reality to unfold as it is, without gap or separation between appearance and reality.
topics: the self that is only the self

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Thanks everybody.
Let's see if I can get everybody on the screen here.
Good evening.
Thank you all for coming as we venture into more Dogen.
I want to continue the summer series of Dogen, and I entitled this talk "The Self That Is Only the Self."
That actually comes from Uchiyama Roshi, who did the commentary on Bendoa.
He is Shohaku Okumura's teacher, if anybody knows who Shohaku is.
This wholehearted way, this Bendoa, is a very short little piece, and it's in the beginning of the book.
Then Uchiyama does this whole commentary, which we've been studying.
A lot of the quotes, I'll try to say which is Dogen and which is Uchiyama as I go along, but a lot of the quotes are from the commentary too.
How are they related?
Uchiyama did the commentary on Dogen's Bendoa, and Shohaku Okumura, who we've studied often, many of us, did the translation.
So it's kind of all three of them.
Right now my teacher, Ryushin Andrea Thatch, and our small cohort of students are studying Bendoa.
Our group moves very slowly, savoring and pondering each paragraph.
It's taken us many months.
We meet once a month, and it's taken many months just to get through these short paragraphs.
It's really wonderful because it gives us time to soak up the meaning.
We stop at many paragraphs and allow them to be kind of stepping-off points for our exploration.
Tonight I want to talk about Bendoa a little bit and the commentary, and maybe some of you may gain an interest in it from the short work, if you haven't already explored it.
I don't know how many people have read it.
I really like it.
Bendoa was written in 1231, right after Fukanzazengi and shortly after he returned from China back to Japan.
I think Fukanzazengi is much more of a practical manual for zazen, but I feel like Bendoa is more about the joy of zazen, on the cushion and in our lives in general.
It's about the underlying reality that we already are the way.
We're already in the way.
We're never apart from the way.
We're never separate from the way that is in all beings.
Dogen often emphasizes the joy of zazen.
The first paragraph of Bendoa reads:
*All Buddha Tathagatas together have been simply transmitting wondrous Dharma and actualizing Anuttara Samyaksambodhi for which there is an unsurpassable, unfabricated, wondrous method.
This method, which has been transmitted only from Buddha to Buddha without deviation, has its criterion Jijuyusamai.*
I don't know how many people have heard that word, but Dogen used it a lot.
One of his followers, many hundreds of years later, wrote a whole book called Jijuyusamai, in honor of Dogen.
In a sec I'll tell you what it means.
One of the translations for Jijuyusamai is Self-fulfillment Dharma Joy Samadhi.
That word itself just feels joyous whenever it comes up in Dogen's work.
I want to think about Dogen's phrase also that many of us know from a different fascicle: "To study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be informed by myriad things."
In the context of our discussion on the self that is only the self, I want to keep that in mind, this study of the self.
The next paragraph or two are from Dogen's Bendoa also.
*Disporting oneself freely in the Samadhi of self-fulfillment Dharma Joy and practicing zazen in an upright posture is the true gate.*
Chris mentioned that last week, the true gate.
*Although this Dharma is abundantly inherent in each person, it is not manifested without practice.*
That's what Dogen found out when he went on his journey to China.
That was his question: if it's already in me, why do I need to practice?
So it really is not manifested without practice, Dogen says.
*It's not attained without realization.
When you let go, the Dharma fills your hands.
It is not within the boundary of one or many.
When you try to speak, it fills your mouth.
It is not limited to vertical or horizontal.
Buddhas continuously dwell in and maintain this Dharma, yet no trace of conceptualization remains.
Living beings constantly function in and use this Dharma, yet it does not appear in their perception.*
I think that is an important statement.
It's always there.
The conditioned self doesn't really recognize it, but the wider self always is there.
It recognizes all of the conditioned self.
That's, I don't know.
*So the wholehearted practice of the way that I'm talking about allows things to exist in enlightenment and enables us to live out oneness in the path of emancipation.
When we break through the barrier and drop off all limitations, we are no longer concerned with these conceptual distinctions.*
I remember a quote from my then teacher, Eileen Quiera, from Mountain Lamp.
She said something like, "The great reality is continuously manifesting itself through each of us."
I got this image, and I remember doing a journal page about that.
The great reality manifesting itself through each of us is a deeper truth.
As we read in the commentary of Bendoa by Uchiyama Roshi, he keeps bringing up what we are all living out, the self that is only the self.
What does that mean, the self that is only the self?
How could it be otherwise?
In Zen, we often talk about the two truths: the truth that we live in a conditioned world and the truth that we are always also in the unconditioned.
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
As Dogen says, form is form and emptiness is emptiness.
So when we talk about the self that is only the self, is it the conditioned self or the unconditioned self?
Is it both?
Is it one?
We are going to explore a little bit.
When we look at the world of the conditioned, we sometimes think that the world is one world and we are on the stage.
Bendoa talks about how we look at a cup on the table at the same time as our partner, and for instance, we think we are seeing the same cup, experiencing the same cup as well as the same backdrop.
As I was writing this, I was sitting on a lovely deck in the mountains at the height of summer, with the smell of pines and the sound of wind in the trees.
I may think that I am experiencing the same thing as my spouse, who was also sitting there.
But my experience, and thus my world, is unique to me.
It's not the same as his.
It never is.
His whole world, his whole life, are unique to him, and my world is to me.
I am experiencing everything through this self that is only the self.
This unique self contains all of my perceptions, my delusions, my fears, also my joys, my aspirations, my understanding.
Uchiyama says:
*Everyone is born within the world of the self only, lives out life with the original life force of the self that is only the self, and dies with the whole world.
This is an extraordinary idea from a common point of view.
You cannot understand it easily, but it is true.
As a matter of fact, whether you understand it or not, whether you believe it is so or not, it is reality.*

*In the same manner, when we study the Buddha Dharma, to study Buddhist terminology, intellectual study is not nearly enough.* Uchiyama says *we should study life itself, which exists as a foundation of Buddhism.
We never actually live within the common society we create through reifying abstract concepts as we usually believe.
We must thoroughly become a person living out the self that is only the self, or we cannot embody the genuine Buddha Dharma.*
You may be thinking, but how could we not live out the self that is only the self?
We only have this one life to experience everything, and in a sense this is true.
However, if we're lost in distraction, if we're not really here in this present unfolding, we're not really experiencing that life.
Uchiyama Roshi says:
*Although we always think we're really living, as a matter of fact, we're not living out the reality of life.
It's essential to become aware of that fact.
Well then, in what way are we living?
In a word, each and every one of us lives by treating abstract concepts as real.*
We live in a fabricated life, filtered through our delusions, our fantasies, preconceived notions, factors handed down through generations.
I remember Thich Nhat Hanh always talking about being present to eat your hamburger.
If you're distracted by your movie or something on the phone or thinking about something you're going to do in the future, you're mis-experiencing your hamburger completely.
It's gone before you know it, and you don't even remember experiencing it.
We're living out this life that is unique to each of us, including our delusions, including our misperceptions, our conditioning.
But as we practice with studying the self with mindful awareness, we can see how these constructs influence and color our world.

When we have an awareness around the way our mind works, it's easier to be present for the deeper self that is only the self, the ground of our being that is connected with everything, the great reality itself.
We're never apart from this.
In our small self that is only the self, we have preferences and opinions and concepts.
This is the world of conditions.
But as we practice, we open to a self without preferences, where there are no opinions or labeling or ideas.
We continue with these human thoughts bubbling up, but we realize that our constant thinking processes are, as Uchiyama Roshi calls them, brain secretions.
We're not trying to get rid of those brain secretions, but we are trying to open the hand of thought.
That was another really famous saying that Uchiyama said, opening the hand of thought.
He says that about all of our thoughts, all of our intellectual comings and goings, just letting them come in and letting them go.
We're not trying to stop them, we're not trying to change them.
He says that some popular writers during the Meiji period in Japan, according to him, taught to attain enlightenment by transforming delusion.
However, Uchiyama says this is not correct.
It may be easier to understand, but it is not what Buddhism teaches.
*In Buddhism, the dichotomy of delusion and enlightenment is transcended from the very beginning.
We have to practice and actualize right now, right here, the Buddha-Dharma reality of life that transcends both delusion and enlightenment.
This is great enlightenment.*
Uchiyama is pointing to a place that's deeper than comparisons, always there but unrecognized by the discriminating mind.
There are many layers of realization and understanding, and when my mother died, I don't know how this happened.
For four days, I was living in a deeper place than my usual constructs.
I was being held by a place in myself where all the trivial dynamics of the relationship with my mom were completely non-existent.
I was experiencing every action from a place below the waves, from a deep place of love.
It wasn't as though I couldn't function or stop thinking.
I was doing everything from this free-flowing place.
Everything I did as I prepared for her memorial, I did it from that place.
Somehow it was such a gift, and I knew that I wouldn't be in that place forever.
It showed me that everything comes and goes, and I believe that even when there is a deeper realization, it's not permanent.
It's not unchanging.
It was a mystery to me.
I didn't will myself to be in that place.
That's what Dogen believed, too, that is continuous practice and why it's so important.
So many people felt that if you can have a great enlightenment, that's it.
You're done.
It's there forever.
But he asked people then, why did the Buddha continue sitting for the rest of his life?
Why did Bodhidharma sit for eight years at the wall?
So he felt that it wasn't.
It's always continuous.
It's never-ending.
And that's how we continue, how we continue deeper.
Here's a bit more of Dogen's words from Bendoa.

*When one displays the Buddha-mudra with one's whole body and mind sitting upright in this samadhi, even for a short time, everything in the entire Dharma world becomes Buddha-mudra, and all space in the universe becomes complete, completely becomes enlightenment.
Therefore, it enables Buddha Tathagatas to increase the Dharma joy of their own original grounds and renew the adornment of the way of awakening.
Simultaneously, all living beings of the Dharma world in the ten directions and six realms become clear and pure in body and mind, realize great emancipation, and their own original face appears.
At that time, all things together awaken to supreme enlightenment and utilize Buddha body, immediately going beyond the culmination of awakening and sitting upright under the kingly Bodhi tree.
At the same time, they turn the incomparable great Dharma wheel and begin expressing ultimate and unfabricated wisdom.*
I remember often reading, when the Buddha had the great enlightenment, what he said is, "I, together with all beings," and it's that.
There is nothing, there is no separation in the deeper way.
This quote by Dogen is reflecting the understanding that within the larger self that is only the self, this Buddha nature is innate within everything.
It includes the separate self that is unique to each of us, but is universal.
We don't each have a unique Buddha nature.
We are all part of this universal Buddha nature.
That is why when one of us awakens, we all awaken.
Dogen continues:

*Therefore, even if only one person sits for a short time, because this zazen is one with all existence and completely permeates all time, it performs everlasting Buddha guidance within the inexhaustible Dharma world in the past, present, and future.
Zazen is equally the same practice and the same enlightenment for both the person sitting and for all Dharmas.
The melodious sound continues to resonate as it echoes, not only during sitting practice, but before and after striking sunyata.*
I thought that was a bell.
I can remember what that meant.
But sunyata means emptiness and more clearly means the complete interdependence of all things, which continues endlessly before and after the hammer hits it.
So I like that thought.
In his teachings, Dogen really emphasized that Buddha nature is inherent in all things, not just me, not just humans, not just sentient beings, but all things.
He says:

*At this time, because earth, grasses and trees, fences and walls, tiles and pebbles, all things in the Dharma realm in ten directions, because they all carry out Buddha work, everyone receives the benefit of wind and water movement causing this functioning, and all are imperceptibly helped by the wondrous and incomprehensible influence of Buddha to actualize the enlightenment at hand.*
Uchiyama says:
*We study Buddha Dharma on the basis of our own lives, and we practice zazen on the basis of Buddha Dharma.
Having this attitude is a crucial matter, for in many cases people do not think of or look at their own lives.
Therefore, they cannot understand the Buddha Dharma.
In the end, even if they practice zazen, they deviate from genuine zazen.
We sit as the self of the entirety of Dharmas, as Dogen Zenji said.
Sitting as the self that is only the self, we sit with Jijuyu Zanmai.
Since zazen is Jijuyu Zanmai, all the myriad Dharmas lie within the self.
Therefore, the self allows everything to become enlightened, and everything allows the self to become enlightened.
This is true awakening and awakening of others.
The enlightenment of Jijuyu Zanmai lacks not even one speck of dust.
The standard of enlightenment never ceases to be actualized.*
For me, this is an inspiration to continuously study the self and continuously practice zazen.
It is not the goal of attaining something, but for the joy of practice realization.
By observing my mind and my thoughts, my concepts and ideas, slowly I can release my grip on everything and open this hand of thought.
I think that the more I genuinely live my unique life in awareness, the more I open my life to this underlying greater self that is always here.
Uchiyama Roshi says:
*For a true practitioner, there should be no gap between outward appearance and reality.
This is especially important for a person who practices zazen as the self that is only the self.*
He talked about teachers here, too: people that perform, that have an appearance that's different from their true practice, and how that doesn't work so well.
*So to practice zazen is to practice the reality of self.
If reality and outer appearance are different, the person's practice is no good at all.
There is no success and failure in the reality of the self.
Just be as it is.
We are totally liberated.
The self that is only the self is absolute enlightenment, and yet as the original life force, it possesses original practice in its original face.
Just be the original life force and keep going on to practice to purify yourself endlessly with this life force.
This is true practice.
When we practice the reality of self that is absolute enlightenment to the end, enlightenment and practice cannot be separate.
Practice and enlightenment are one.*
And that's why we hear so often from Dogen about practice enlightenment.

Sitting as the self that is only the self, we sit with Jijuyu Zanmai. Since zazen is Jijuyu Zanmai, all the myriad Dharmas lie within the self. Therefore, the self allows everything to become enlightened, and everything allows the self to become enlightened. This is true awakening and awakening of others. The enlightenment of Jijuyu Zanmai lacks not even one speck of dust. The standard of enlightenment never ceases to be actualized. For me, this is an inspiration to continuously study the self and continuously practice zazen. It is not the goal of attaining something, but for the joy of practice realization.

By observing my mind and my thoughts, my concepts and ideas, slowly I can release my grip on everything and open this hand of thought. I think that the more I genuinely live my unique life in awareness, the more I open my life to this underlying greater self that is always here. Uchiyama Aroshi says, For a true practitioner, there should be no gap between outward appearance and reality. This is especially important for a person who practices zazen as the self that is only the self. He talked about teachers here, too. People that perform, that have an appearance that's different from their true practice and how that doesn't work so well.

So to practice zazen is to practice the reality of self. If reality and outer appearance are different, the person's practice is no good at all. There is no success and failure in the reality of the self. Just be as it is. We are totally liberated. The self that is only the self is absolute enlightenment, and yet as the original life force, it possesses original practice in its original face. Just be the original life force and keep going on to practice to purify yourself endlessly with this life force. This is true practice.

When we practice the reality of self that is absolute enlightenment to the end, enlightenment and practice cannot be separate. Practice and enlightenment are one. And so that's why we hear so often from Dogen about practice enlightenment.
